 Intense flooding slams Florida from a developing storm that could snarl early Thanksgiving travel on the East Coast
 By Meteorologists Dakota Smith , Chris Dolce , and CNN's Holly Yan , Sara Smart 
 Updated Nov 18, 2026, 1:33 PM ET 
 PUBLISHED Nov 18, 2026, 7:30 AM ET 
 Motorists drive through floodwater in Hollywood, Florida, on November 18. 
 Joe Raedle/Getty Images 
 Storms 
 Oceania

 Torrential rainfall and severe flooding shut down roads, gushed into homes and forced high-water rescues in southeast Florida overnight as a multi-day flood threat unfolds along the state’s Atlantic coast.
 ⛈️ ☔️ Track the storm and get your local forecast in the CNN Weather app . 
 Parts of the northern Miami metro area, including Broward County, suffered the most significant rainfall. Over a foot of rain — more than three Novembers’ worth — fell in mere hours in the Hollywood area, with some places getting walloped by more than 5 inches of rain per hour, the National Weather Service in Miami said.
 Hollywood’s mayor declared a state of emergency and urged residents to shelter in place as the torrent closed parts of Interstate 95 and Florida’s Turnpike . First responders received more than 300 calls for service between 11 p.m. and 4 a.m., the Hollywood Police Department said, and high-water vehicles were still deployed late Wednesday morning.
 The ferocious rainfall caused the roof to collapse at the Temple Sinai in Hollywood, police said. No injuries were reported.
 Daniel Supienski and his daughter Dezirae Supienski paddle down a flooded street in a kayak near their home in Hollywood, Florida, on November 18. 
 Joe Raedle/Getty Images 
 Aerial views of flooding in Broward County. 
 WSVN 
 The deluge has also forced schools to shutter, including several campuses of Keiser University. All Broward County Public Schools were closed Wednesday, and the status of Thursday’s classes “will be shared later today,” the school district said.
 Broward County declared a state of emergency Wednesday, as did Fort Lauderdale. City officials said residents could protect their cars by parking them in the upper levels of a public parking garage for free.
 Extreme rainfall like this is becoming more frequent as the world warms due to fossil fuel pollution. A warmer atmosphere can soak up more moisture like a sponge and wring it out in the form of gushing rainfall.
 More flash flooding is possible in southeast Florida over the next few days, but the biggest area of concern will shift north and include parts of the Space Coast that were inundated with historic rainfall and severe flooding earlier this month.
 A computer model depiction of the rainfall timing from Wednesday afternoon into Friday afternoon. 
 CNN Weather 
 Some rivers are still high in those areas, which are vulnerable to flooding from the additional rain. Winds blowing onshore and high surf will also pound the Florida coast in coming days, producing dangerous rip currents and potentially major beach erosion.
 After drenching Florida, this budding storm will head north, where it’s likely to throw a wrench in travel during the busy pre-Thanksgiving weekend. It will linger off the Southeast coast until Saturday, when it’ll begin to push farther north.
 The storm’s East Coast impacts into early next week will depend on its path, which forecast models are still working to suss out.
 Florida’s multiday deluge
 Florida’s eastern coast faces three consecutive days of a Level 3 out of 4 flood risk through Friday.
 A widespread 3 to 6 inches of rain is expected to fall across eastern Florida through Friday, with 8 to 12 inches or more possible in some areas along the state’s eastern coast. A foot of rain in some locations, like Daytona Beach, would mean four Novembers’ worth of rain fell in just a few days.
 Pinpointing the exact communities that might endure those higher-end totals is challenging and will depend on where storms form and stall out with torrential rain for several hours.
 Melbourne, Florida – the epicenter of the historic rainfall earlier this month – is in the highest flood threat area on Wednesday and Thursday. The city just had its rainiest day on record on November 2 after 11.5 inches fell there. Melbourne is about 8 inches shy of its rainiest year on record, which could happen during this week’s storm.
 On Friday, the Level 3 of 4 flood risk stretches farther north to near the Florida-Georgia state line, as seen in purple below. Here, rainfall rates greater than 2 inches an hour are possible, which would add significantly to rainfall totals from the two previous days and increase the chances for serious flooding.
 Wetter than normal periods are not a surprise in Florida this fall and winter as the super El Niño continues to strengthen, changing global weather patterns and increasing storm chances across the US Southeast.
 Holiday travel threat could emerge
 Forecast models are still sorting out exactly where the storm will go after Florida, but there are two favored scenarios at this time, both of which could impact travel starting this weekend. Last year, the weekend prior to Thanksgiving was one of the busiest travel periods of the holiday week, according to TSA screening data .
 Scenario 1: The storm tracks near or into the Southeast coast this weekend and then darts into the Northeast by Monday, bringing a sloppy mix of rain, wind and possibly coastal flooding with it.
 This track could cause airport delays and create treacherous travel on roads, including along the parts of highly traveled Interstate 95.
 Scenario 2: The storm stays along the the Southeast coast, delivering rain, wind and coastal flooding to the region before heading out to sea, minimizing its impacts farther north along the East Coast.
 Right now, it’s looking like the first scenario is most likely, but that could change as the forecast comes into focus later this week.
 The two main scenarios for the storm's track this weekend into Monday. 
 CNN Weather 
 There’s also a medium chance the system could eventually transition into a fully tropical or hybrid storm if it remains over water long enough, according to the National Hurricane Center.
 But, that possible designation makes little difference when it comes to impacts: the storm will bring strong winds, heavy rain and coastal flooding either way.
 Kyle will be the name of the Atlantic hurricane season’s next storm.
 CNN’s Hanna Park and Jeremy Grisham contributed to this report.
